c.entradas.descenso-inanna.nombre: The Descent of Inanna to the Underworld
c.entradas.descenso-inanna.nombre_origin: an gal-ta ki gal-še3 (Sumerian, 'From the great heaven to the great earth'); ETCSL 1.4.1; Akkadian version: Descent of Ishtar
c.entradas.descenso-inanna.fecha_texto: Sumerian version: Old Babylonian copies, c. 1900–1700 BC. Akkadian version, much shorter: Middle Assyrian and Neo-Assyrian copies from Assur and Nineveh.
c.entradas.descenso-inanna.resumen: Inanna descends to the Underworld, where her sister Ereshkigal reigns. At each of its seven gates she loses a garment or a jewel, until she is killed and her corpse is hung on a hook. Enki brings her back to life, but to leave she must put someone in her place, and she chooses her husband Dumuzi.
c.entradas.descenso-inanna.interpretacio:
The myth deals with the limits of divine power: not even the most ambitious goddess can escape death without paying a price. Jacobsen and others linked it to agricultural and pastoral cycles and to ritual laments for Dumuzi. Today the old Frazer-style reading of the 'dying and rising god' is avoided: Dumuzi's return only appears at the end, when he and his sister Geshtinanna divide the year between them.

It has also been read in political and cultic terms, as a ritual in which the goddess's statue visits another shrine. The stripping of her insignia at each gate has been interpreted as the loss of Inanna's me. The Akkadian version (Descent of Ishtar) lacks the Dumuzi episodes, and the text was used in rites of the month of Du'uzu (Tammuz).
c.entradas.descenso-inanna.detalles.0: The Sumerian text has about 410 lines.
c.entradas.descenso-inanna.detalles.1: Before descending, Inanna instructs her servant Ninshubur to seek help if she does not return.
c.entradas.descenso-inanna.detalles.2: Enlil and Nanna refuse to help. Enki creates two beings, the kurgara and the galatura, who revive her with the food and water of life.
c.entradas.descenso-inanna.detalles.3: The galla demons pursue Dumuzi, who ends up as Inanna's substitute.
c.entradas.descenso-inanna.detalles.4: In the end, Dumuzi and his sister Geshtinanna take turns spending half the year each in the Underworld.
c.entradas.descenso-inanna.fuentes_prima: Tablets from Nippur and Ur (Sumerian, Old Babylonian)
Library of Ashurbanipal, Nineveh (Descent of Ishtar)
c.entradas.enki-ninhursag.fecha_texto: Old Babylonian copies from Nippur and Ur, c. 1900–1700 BC. There is a version from Ur with variants.
c.entradas.enki-ninhursag.resumen: On the pure island of Dilmun, Enki brings fresh water and unites in turn with Ninhursag, with her daughter and with her granddaughter. Then he eats eight plants that the goddess had made sprout. Ninhursag curses him and Enki falls ill, until she agrees to heal him by giving birth to eight deities, one for each aching part of his body.
c.entradas.enki-ninhursag.interpretacion:
The myth combines fertility (fresh water and earth), etiology, which explains the origin of certain plants and deities, and wordplay: the god born to heal each part of the body bears a name related to it. Ninti, 'the lady of the rib', is the most frequently cited example.

Kramer compared it with the biblical Eden because of the paradise of Dilmun, the forbidden plant and the rib, since Sumerian 'ti' means both 'rib' and 'life'. Today these parallels are considered suggestive but do not prove direct dependence. Dilmun, identified with Bahrain, represents an ideal, primordial place here.
c.entradas.enki-ninhursag.detalles.0: The story begins in Dilmun, where there is not yet any sickness or old age.
c.entradas.enki-ninhursag.detalles.1: Enki unites with Ninhursag (Ninnisig), then with Ninsar, with Ninkurra and finally with Uttu, goddess of weaving.
c.entradas.enki-ninhursag.detalles.2: Enki eats eight plants before they have been given a name or a destiny.
c.entradas.enki-ninhursag.detalles.3: Ninhursag heals Enki by giving birth to, among others, Ninti, 'lady of the rib' or 'lady of life'.
c.entradas.enki-ninhursag.fuentes_primar: Old Babylonian tablets from Nippur (Penn Museum)
c.entradas.enki-orden-mundo.nombre_origi: Enki and the World Order (Sumerian); ETCSL 1.1.3
c.entradas.enki-orden-mundo.fecha_texto: Old Babylonian copies, c. 1900–1700 BC, mainly from Nippur.
c.entradas.enki-orden-mundo.resumen: Enki travels through Sumer and the neighboring lands and decrees the destiny of each region. He organizes the rivers, agriculture, herding and the crafts, and puts a god in charge of each domain. At the end, Inanna complains that she has not been given any function, and Enki grants her several.
c.entradas.enki-orden-mundo.interpretaci:
It is a narrative hymn of about 470 lines that celebrates Enki as the god who organizes civilization. It distributes the functions of the gods and describes the Sumerian world in orderly fashion: Sumer, Ur, Meluhha, Dilmun, Elam and Martu. Scholars read it as a 'theological geography' and connect it with the tradition of the me, the divine norms of cultural order.

Inanna's complaint reflects a tension that also appears in 'Inanna and Enki': the goddess claims her powers, a theme that may reflect the growing importance of her cult in Uruk.
c.entradas.enki-orden-mundo.detalles.1: Enki fills the Tigris and the Euphrates with water 'like a bull'.
c.entradas.enki-orden-mundo.detalles.2: He assigns different domains to deities such as Enbilulu (canals), Ashnan (grain), Kabta (hoe and brick mold) and Utu (justice).
c.entradas.enki-orden-mundo.detalles.3: The poem's geography includes Meluhha, in the Indus Valley, and Dilmun.
c.entradas.lista-reyes.nombre_original: nam-lugal an-ta e11-de3-a-ba (Sumerian, 'When kingship came down from heaven')
c.entradas.lista-reyes.fecha_texto: The oldest version dates to Ur III (c. 2100 BC). Most copies are Old Babylonian; the Weld-Blundell prism is dated c. 1800 BC (reign of Sin-magir of Isin).
c.entradas.lista-reyes.resumen: It is a list of cities and kings that, according to the text, received in turn the kingship 'lowered from heaven'. It begins in Eridu and runs down to the dynasty of Isin. It assigns the kings before the flood reigns of tens of thousands of years.
c.entradas.lista-reyes.interpretacion:
It is an ideological composition, not a reliable chronicle. It argues that Mesopotamia could have only one legitimate center of kingship at a time. In reality, many of the dynasties it presents as successive were contemporary. The kings of Isin used it to present themselves as the legitimate heirs of Ur III.

The antediluvian section and the flood do not appear in the Ur III version and were added in the Old Babylonian period. The enormous reign lengths are explained by conventions of the sexagesimal system and by the idea that primordial times were different. It mixes legendary figures, such as Etana, Lugalbanda, Dumuzi or Gilgamesh, with kings attested in inscriptions.
c.entradas.lista-reyes.detalles.0: The Weld-Blundell prism (WB 444, Ashmolean Museum, Oxford), from c. 1800 BC, is the most complete copy.
c.entradas.lista-reyes.detalles.1: In that copy, eight antediluvian kings in five cities total 241,200 years.
c.entradas.lista-reyes.detalles.2: The first king is Alulim of Eridu.
c.entradas.lista-reyes.detalles.3: After the flood, kingship passes to Kish, where Etana appears as the shepherd 'who ascended to heaven'.
c.entradas.lista-reyes.detalles.4: There is an Ur III version without an antediluvian section, preserved on a tablet perhaps from Adab.
c.entradas.lista-reyes.fuentes_primarias: Weld-Blundell prism, Ashmolean Museum (provenance attributed to Larsa)
Tablets from Nippur, Isin and other cities
c.entradas.anzu.nombre_original: Anzû (Akkadian; in Sumerian, Anzud, formerly read Imdugud)
c.entradas.anzu.fecha_texto: Old Babylonian version (early 2nd millennium BC, copy from Susa). The longer Standard Babylonian version is known from Neo-Assyrian copies from Nineveh and elsewhere (8th–7th centuries BC).
c.entradas.anzu.resumen: The monstrous bird Anzu steals the Tablet of Destinies from Enlil while the god is bathing, and thereby paralyzes the order of the universe. No god dares to face it until Ninurta, advised by Ea and by his mother, defeats it and returns the tablet.
c.entradas.anzu.interpretacion:
It is a combat myth that exalts Ninurta (Ningirsu in the Lagash tradition) as champion of the gods. The Tablet of Destinies symbolizes supreme authority over the universe. The Enuma Elish reuses this structure: the assembly of the gods finds no one willing to fight, a young hero wins, and his victory brings exaltation.

In Assyria, Ninurta was a very important warrior god. Ashurnasirpal II built his temple in Kalhu (Nimrud), and the reliefs from that temple show a god pursuing a winged monster, an image usually connected with this myth. In early Sumerian iconography, Anzu appears as a lion-headed eagle, the emblem of Ningirsu in Lagash.
c.entradas.anzu.detalles.0: Enlil loses the Tablet of Destinies while bathing.
c.entradas.anzu.detalles.1: Adad, Girra and Shara refuse, one after another, to fight Anzu.
c.entradas.anzu.detalles.2: In the Old Babylonian version, the hero is Ningirsu.
c.entradas.anzu.detalles.3: Ea advises Ninurta to cut off Anzu's wings to defeat it.
c.entradas.anzu.detalles.4: The Stele of the Vultures of Eannatum of Lagash (c. 2450 BC) shows the lion-headed eagle emblem.
c.entradas.anzu.fuentes_primarias.1: Neo-Assyrian copies from Nineveh and Sultantepe
c.entradas.anzu.fuentes_primarias.2: Relief from the temple of Ninurta at Kalhu (Nimrud), British Museum
c.entradas.erra-ishum.nombre_original: Erra u Išum (Akkadian); sometimes called the Erra Epic
c.entradas.erra-ishum.fecha_texto: It is usually dated to the 8th century BC; some propose a date between the 11th and 9th centuries BC (debated). The copies are mainly Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian.
c.entradas.erra-ishum.resumen: Erra, god of war and plague, persuades Marduk to leave his throne to have his image restored. He takes advantage of his absence to unleash violence and destruction on Babylon and other cities. His adviser Ishum manages to calm him, and Erra ends by promising that the land will recover.
c.entradas.erra-ishum.interpretacion:
It is one of the most original works of Akkadian literature. It is read as a theological response to a time of crisis in Babylonia (invasions, disorder and raids by Arameans and Suteans): it explains the disaster as the fury of a god who acted while Marduk was absent. It fills five tablets. The colophon says that its author, Kabti-ilani-Marduk, received it in a dream and wrote it down without changing anything.

The text had an apotropaic use: excerpts were copied onto amulets to protect houses and people from plague. It is a clear example of how religious literature served magical and protective functions.
c.entradas.erra-ishum.detalles.0: It has five tablets and about 750 lines.
c.entradas.erra-ishum.detalles.1: The author, Kabti-ilani-Marduk, appears in the catalog of texts and authors from Nineveh.
c.entradas.erra-ishum.detalles.2: Ishum, Erra's adviser and herald, acts as mediator.
c.entradas.erra-ishum.detalles.3: Tablet-shaped amulets bearing passages of the poem have been found.
Tablets from Assur, Sultantepe and Babylon
Amulets with excerpts from the text
c.entradas.adapa.nombre_original: Adapa (Akkadian); also called 'the sage' (apkallu) of Eridu
c.entradas.adapa.fecha_texto: The oldest fragment comes from Tell el-Amarna, in Egypt (14th century BC). There are Neo-Assyrian copies from Nineveh from the 7th century BC and an Old Babylonian Sumerian fragment from Tell Haddad.
c.entradas.adapa.resumen: Adapa, sage and priest of Ea in Eridu, breaks the wing of the South Wind when it capsizes his boat while he is fishing. Anu summons him to heaven. Ea advises him not to accept the bread or the water he is offered, because they will be 'of death'. Anu in fact offers him the bread and water of life, and Adapa, by refusing them, loses immortality.
c.entradas.adapa.interpretacion:
The central theme is why human beings, even the wisest, remain mortal. It is debated whether Ea deliberately deceived Adapa so that immortality would stay out of human reach or whether he made an unintended mistake; the ambiguity seems to be part of the work. It has been compared with Genesis 3 and with Gilgamesh.

Adapa is often identified with Uanna-Adapa, the first of the seven sages (apkallu) of the tradition, later known to Berossus as Oannes. The Amarna copy shows that this text was used to train scribes at foreign courts.
c.entradas.adapa.detalles.0: The Amarna tablet has red ink dots marking word divisions, an aid for scribes who did not speak Akkadian.
c.entradas.adapa.detalles.1: Anu's doorkeepers are Dumuzi and Ningishzida, who intercede on Adapa's behalf.
c.entradas.adapa.detalles.2: The ending preserved in the Nineveh copies is fragmentary.
c.entradas.adapa.fuentes_primarias.0: Tablet from Tell el-Amarna (Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin)
c.entradas.adapa.fuentes_primarias.1: Fragments from the Library of Ashurbanipal, Nineveh
